To be able to send a photograph and get an answer
personas.fears: Wasting time; being handled by a system; discovering later that nobody was actually responsible.
killers: A long form as the only route
A page that takes three screens to say what it does
personas.servedBy: The hero and the persistent contact control. The existing hero — 'From an idea, a photograph, a sample or a drawing — to mass production' — is close to ideal for this persona: it names the input they actually have rather than the input a supplier would prefer. This is also the persona for whom WhatsApp is exactly right in Turkey, the Gulf and South Asia, and exactly wrong in Russia, China and Thailand.

personasOnOnePage.principle: Do not build four sections for four personas. Build ONE spine with four depths, and let each reader stop where their job ends. Bloat comes from repeating the argument at four levels of abstraction; depth comes from continuing the same argument into greater specificity.
mechanism: Depth 1 — the hero. One sentence naming the input the buyer already has. Serves the owner/CEO completely; everyone else scrolls past it in two seconds.
Depth 2 — the route. Five stages, one accountable partner. Serves the production manager and orients everyone else. Already built.

Depth 3 — expandable engineering detail inside each stage. Serves the engineer. Invisible to those who do not open it, so it costs the other three personas nothing. The 'more detail / less detail' toggle already exists in common.json — this is what it is for.

Depth 4 — a quiet commercial band near the foot: quote structure, payment staging, tooling ownership, response window, delivery, one ungated download. Serves procurement. Deliberately unglamorous and deliberately last, because the CEO does not need it and the procurement manager will scroll to find it.
personasOnOnePage.sharedElements: One persistent contact control with two channels of equal weight. One language switcher. One factual footer with address, and a working week. Nothing else appears twice.
personasOnOnePage.antiBloatRule: Every new block must answer a question a named persona would actually ask, in words that persona would use. If it answers no question, it is decoration; if it answers a question already answered, it is repetition. Both should be cut. A shorter page with four real depths outperforms a longer page with four restatements.

whatSeriousBuyersActuallyExpect: That an NDA is offered BEFORE they are asked for files, not after they ask for one. Volunteering it is the signal; the document itself is close to worthless across this particular border.
That they are not required to disclose everything to get a first answer. The most reassuring thing a supplier can offer is a smaller first disclosure, not a bigger promise.

A NON-USE undertaking, not merely non-disclosure. Harris Sliwoski's core finding: a conventional NDA covers disclosure of trade secrets and leaves competitive USE of non-secret information wide open. Buyers who have been burned know this distinction; buyers who have not still respond to the plainer sentence.

Clarity on who owns the CAD — including native editable files, and including improvements the supplier proposes. Harris Sliwoski: 'all upgrades — regardless of who proposed or implemented them — belong to the original owner unless expressly agreed otherwise.'

That subcontractors are bound. Undisclosed mould-shop subcontracting is named as a red-flag behaviour, and it is how designs leak in practice — not through the supplier, through the supplier's supplier.
That the supplier will not file design or patent applications on the buyer's part. Named explicitly as a hostage tactic.
That the agreement names the correct registered legal entity, in the correct language, sealed correctly. This is the difference between a document and a gesture.
That the physical tool is marked with their identifier and segregated from other customers' tooling.
credibleWording: 'You do not need to send a full CAD package to get a first answer. A photograph and one dimension is enough to say whether it is worth going further.'
'An NDA can be signed before any detailed technical disclosure.' — the exact confirmed claim; use it verbatim.

'Your drawings, models and samples are used to quote your part and build your tool. They are not used to make the same part for anyone else, and they are not shown to another customer.' — non-use, stated plainly, no legal vocabulary.
'Improvements we suggest to your part belong to your part.'

'Native and neutral CAD (STEP, IGES) for your tool is yours, and you can have it at any time — not only when the relationship ends.' — the timing clause is the tell that the supplier has thought about this properly.
'No part of your tool is subcontracted without your written approval.'
'Your tool carries your tool number and is stored separately from other customers' tooling.'

'This is written into the order, not into this page.' — the single best closing line for this whole section. It moves the promise from marketing to contract, which is exactly where the buyer wants it.
redFlagWording: 'We respect your intellectual property.' Says nothing, costs nothing, means nothing, and is what every site says.
'100% confidential' / 'your design is completely safe with us.' Absolutes on an unenforceable promise read as the opposite of confidence.
'Our NDA is legally binding worldwide.' Claims enforceability the supplier cannot deliver, and any buyer with counsel will check.
A downloadable generic NDA PDF as the whole answer. It signals a template, and Harris Sliwoski's position on templates is unambiguous — 'Templates Are Not Contracts: They're Landmines.'
'We have never had an IP dispute.' Unverifiable, and it invites the buyer to imagine the first one.
'All our work is under NDA' as the explanation for having no portfolio. Flagged in claims.ts specifically. It is a recognised tell and buyers discount it automatically.
Long legal paragraphs on a marketing page. Buyers read length here as an attempt to bury something.
Any mention of registering IP in the supplier's own name 'for the customer's protection'. Named directly as a hostage tactic.
ipAndNda.theHonestLimit: Cross-border enforcement from Iran is, realistically, weak in both directions and a serious buyer's counsel will know it. So the site must not compete on legal remedy — it will lose. It should compete on EXPOSURE REDUCTION: staged disclosure so the buyer risks less, non-use stated in plain language so the promise is at least legible, tool marking and segregation so the physical risk is visible, subcontractor control so the leak path is closed, and CAD release on demand so the buyer is never trapped. Every one of those is a mechanism the buyer can verify by observation rather than by litigation. That is the only version of this argument that survives scrutiny.

evidence: Average form length is 5 fields; over 30% of marketers report their highest conversion from 4-field forms; cutting 4 fields to 3 lifts conversion by roughly 50% (HubSpot, Quicksprout via WPForms).

Multi-step forms convert 86% higher than single-step, yet only 40% of marketers use them (HubSpot via WPForms). For industrial RFQs this is the resolution of the whole problem: the information genuinely IS needed, so stage it rather than cut it.

81% of people have abandoned at least one web form. Stated reasons: security concerns 29%, form length 27%, adverts or upselling 11%, unclear purpose of data collection 10% (The Manifest via WPForms). Note that security and unclear purpose together (39%) outweigh length (27%) — for a supplier in an unfamiliar country, the trust problem is larger than the length problem.
Average abandonment occurs at 1 minute 43 seconds (Feathery via WPForms).

Phone and email fields are among the highest-abandonment field types after passwords (Zuko via WPForms). A required phone field on a first-contact form from a foreign supplier is a significant, and avoidable, cost.

84% of people prefer to complete forms on laptop or desktop, and desktop converts at 3% against mobile 2% (The Manifest, Statista via WPForms). But industrial buyers in this specific market frequently arrive on mobile, which is an argument for a non-form channel rather than for a mobile form.
NN/g: registration barriers before credibility is established are a primary reason B2B users leave; substantial information should be available pre-registration.

6sense: buyers make first contact at 61% of the way through the journey, with 94% having already ranked their shortlist. The form is therefore not persuading anyone — it is a toll gate placed in front of a decision that is already made. Every field is a chance to lose a buyer who had already chosen.
rfqFriction.theIndustrialParadox: A useful moulding RFQ genuinely needs 3D geometry, a 2D drawing with GD&T, material grade, quantity tiers, finish, tolerance intent and business terms. RapidDirect's guide is explicit that every missing item becomes a supplier assumption and assumptions are priced conservatively — ambiguous tolerances 'add risk premiums'. So the buyer's interest and the supplier's interest both argue for a LONG form, and the conversion data argues for a short one. Cutting the form does not solve this; it just moves the missing information into the first email.
resolution: Split intake into two artefacts that serve different moments. (1) A two-field opening: what the part is, and how to reach you — plus a file attachment. That is the whole first step. (2) A complete RFQ checklist, published as an ungated page and a downloadable document, for the buyer who is ready.

Make the checklist a gift rather than a demand. Frame it as what it actually is: 'Every blank in an RFQ becomes an assumption, and assumptions get priced conservatively. Here is the list, so you can price the same part fairly with anyone.' The buyer will use it on competitors too — which is fine, because the supplier who taught them to read the quote is the supplier they trust to read it with.
Never require a phone number to start. It is a high-abandonment field and, from an unfamiliar country, it is the specific field that triggers the 29% security concern.
Never gate anything. NN/g is unambiguous that registration barriers before credibility destroy B2B trust, and this site has less credibility to spend than most.

Accept a file attachment on the very first contact. A buyer with a STEP file open is a buyer at maximum intent, and a form that cannot receive it converts intent into friction. WhatsApp handling documents up to 100MB is a genuine, honest advantage here — say so.

State explicitly what an incomplete enquiry gets: 'Send what you have. If something is missing we will tell you what it is and why it changes the answer.' This removes the buyer's fear of asking badly, which is the real reason industrial buyers stall at the form.
Repeat the entry point at the foot of every industry page with a prefill specific to that industry — already the design in WhatsAppButton.astro, which is the right instinct.

whatsappByRegion.summaryJudgement: WhatsApp-first is correct for roughly half of this site's language set and a liability for the other half. Treating it as the universal primary CTA — which is the current architecture, with WhatsAppButton.astro as 'the conversion control' on every page — is a genuine strategic error for ru, zh, th and, in a different way, for European buyers. The fix is not to demote WhatsApp; it is to make the channel a function of locale, and to give email equal weight everywhere.

regions.verdict: WhatsApp-first is correct and should be the primary CTA
regions.evidence: WhatsApp is near-universal in Turkey and fully normalised for business, including B2B supplier contact. Wikipedia lists Turkey among countries with restriction history, but WhatsApp remains the dominant messenger in practice; the 2021 privacy-policy backlash pushed a minority to BiP and Telegram without displacing it.
regions.note: Turkish-language fluency matters more than channel choice here. A Turkish buyer reading translated-sounding Turkish will not message on any channel.

regions.region: Gulf — UAE, Saudi, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman (ar)
regions.verdict: WhatsApp-first for TEXT, but never offer a WhatsApp call
regions.evidence: Wikipedia (Telecommunications in the UAE): 'All or most VoIP services are blocked. Both WhatsApp and Snapchat calling functions were also blocked in the UAE, to comply with VoIP regulations.' The March 2020 partial relaxation still left WhatsApp, FaceTime and Skype blocked. Text messaging is unaffected and is entirely business-normal across the Gulf.
regions.note: A 'call us on WhatsApp' CTA fails outright for a UAE buyer and signals that the supplier does not know the region. Any escalation to voice must be a normal telephone number. This is a small detail with a disproportionate credibility cost.

regions.region: South Asia — India, Pakistan, Bangladesh (ur, en)
regions.evidence: Wikipedia: by 2016 WhatsApp had become 'the primary means of Internet communication' across the Indian subcontinent; India is its largest market. WhatsApp Business is the default channel for SME industrial trade.
regions.note: This is the region where a long RFQ form performs worst and a photo-plus-message intake performs best. The Urdu locale is well judged.

regions.region: South-East Asia — Thailand (th), Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore
regions.verdict: Split. WhatsApp-first is WRONG for Thailand specifically.
regions.evidence: WhatsApp is strong in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore. Thailand is a LINE market, not a WhatsApp market, and Vietnam is a Zalo market — in both, WhatsApp penetration is marginal and a WhatsApp CTA reads as foreign.
regions.note: Since this project ships a Thai locale, the th pages should lead with email and a form, not WhatsApp. If a LINE official account is ever available it belongs here; until then, email is the honest primary.

regions.verdict: WhatsApp is unusable. WeChat or email.
regions.evidence: WhatsApp is blocked in mainland China (listed in Wikipedia's bans section); WeChat is the business channel and is also on Russia's banned-for-government-use list, which is irrelevant here but indicates its reach.
regions.note: CONTACT.wechat already exists as a pending value in site.ts — that is the correct instinct and it is a blocking item for the zh locale. A Chinese-language page whose only CTA is WhatsApp is a page with no CTA.

regions.verdict: WhatsApp is a genuine liability. Email and phone must lead.
regions.evidence: Wikipedia (Internet censorship in Russia): 'By 2026, internet censorship had escalated to the point of widespread mobile Internet outages, VPN restrictions, and the blocking and throttling of Telegram and WhatsApp in favor of the state-controlled Max.' Roskomnadzor was already 'imposing restrictions of the use of WhatsApp' by September 2025. MAX was made the official national messenger on 15 July 2025 and mandatory for pre-installation from 1 September 2025. WhatsApp, Telegram, Viber, Teams, Signal and WeChat are all banned for use in Russian government organisations (2023, 2024).
regions.note: Two separate problems compound here: the channel may not work, and a Russian corporate buyer may be formally prohibited from using it. Email is the only channel that is both reliable and defensible. The ru pages should not lead with a WhatsApp button.

regions.verdict: WhatsApp works, but is not the only default. Offer three.
regions.evidence: Viber has historically been unusually dominant in Armenia and the wider Caucasus, with Telegram and WhatsApp both in common use. ITA: 'Personal contact is key in Armenia'; in-person interaction is standard and 'phone-based support remains uncommon' — meaning the messenger substitutes for a visit rather than for a phone call.
regions.note: Armenia is the most relationship-driven market in the set. The channel matters less than a named human and Armenian-language copy. Note ITA's observation that Armenian is the official language for advertising material, with foreign-language text permitted in smaller script — the hy locale is not optional for this market.

regions.region: Europe (en, plus EU buyers on other locales)
regions.verdict: WhatsApp is a liability as the PRIMARY channel, acceptable as an option
regions.evidence: WhatsApp penetration is very high across Southern and Eastern Europe and high in Germany and the Netherlands, so the channel exists. But European B2B procurement runs on an auditable paper trail: a procurement manager needs a message they can forward to a buying committee, attach to a requisition, and retain. NN/g's B2B research shows business buyers want substantial information and a documented process, and many European companies formally restrict consumer messengers for supplier communication on records-retention and data-protection grounds.
regions.note: 6sense: 94% of buyers have already ranked their shortlist before contact. For a European buyer the first contact is often an internal forward, not a message — and a WhatsApp thread cannot be forwarded into a procurement system.

regions.region: Iran (fa) — and the supplier's own side of every conversation
regions.verdict: Do not build a single-channel dependency in either direction
regions.evidence: Domestic connectivity in Iran is subject to periodic national throttling and shutdown, and WhatsApp access there has itself been blocked and unblocked over recent years. The risk is not only that the buyer cannot reach the channel — it is that the supplier cannot.
regions.note: This is the strongest operational argument for email as a first-class channel rather than a fallback: a hosted mailbox is the only channel that keeps working when the messenger does not, and an enquiry that arrives while the messenger is down is still an enquiry when it comes back. The 48-hour window is only credible if the channel that carries it is resilient.

theDiscreetSecondaryChannel.recommendation: A plain, human email address — a named person, not info@ — displayed at equal visual weight to WhatsApp on every page, in every locale, with no explanation whatsoever.
why: It is forwardable, archivable and attachable to a requisition — the three things a procurement manager needs and no messenger provides.
It leaves no personal mobile number in a foreign supplier's phone, which is a real and almost never-articulated concern for European, Russian and Gulf buyers dealing with an unfamiliar country.
It is channel-neutral: it works identically in Russia, China, Thailand, the Gulf and Europe, where no single messenger does.
It survives connectivity disruption on either side.
It is the discreet option by default, without anyone having to say the word discreet.
theDiscreetSecondaryChannel.howToPresentIt: Silently. Two controls, side by side, equal weight, no labels like 'or contact us privately' and no explanation of why an alternative exists. The moment discretion is named it becomes conspicuous and the buyer starts wondering what they are being protected from. A second button is the whole solution.
theDiscreetSecondaryChannel.secondaryOptions: Telegram for Armenia, Russia, Iran and Central Asia (already pending in site.ts — worth filling). WeChat for China (pending — blocking for zh). A normal telephone number everywhere, and especially for the Gulf where WhatsApp voice does not work.

copyDirectives.rule: Name the country in the first screen
copyDirectives.do: Put the city and country in the hero area or immediately beneath it, and again in the footer. Plain, unhedged, one line.
copyDirectives.dont: Do not let a buyer discover the country in a footer address after three minutes, and do not substitute 'global' or 'international' for the fact.
copyDirectives.because: A hidden origin is assumed to be a concealed origin, and the assumption is always worse than the fact. It also filters unqualified enquiries early, which protects the response window.

copyDirectives.rule: Lead with the part, not the company
copyDirectives.do: Open on what the reader has and what comes back — the existing 'From an idea, a photograph, a sample or a drawing — to mass production' is close to ideal because it names the input the buyer actually possesses.
copyDirectives.dont: Do not open with founding year, values, mission, or 'we are a leading manufacturer of'.
copyDirectives.because: Gate 1 is 'does this supplier's world contain my problem'. A company-first opening answers a question nobody asked and burns the only fifteen seconds available.

copyDirectives.rule: Never render a number without a unit and a period
copyDirectives.do: '1,000+ completed projects since 2006.' 'Tooling experience up to 46 cavities.'
copyDirectives.dont: No '99%', no '500+', no '20 years of excellence', no percentage savings, no satisfaction score.
copyDirectives.because: Round unanchored numbers are read as decoration and, worse, they occupy the position where evidence would be — implying evidence was sought and not found.

copyDirectives.rule: Substitute demonstrated engineering for every credential the site cannot claim
copyDirectives.do: Where a certification would sit, put a decision and its consequence: why a hot runner starts paying above roughly 20–30,000 units; why wall thickness drives cycle time; why a gate moves off a sealing face.
copyDirectives.dont: Do not mention certification at all — not to claim it, not to explain its absence, not to argue that it does not matter.
copyDirectives.because: Certification is a proxy for documented process. The proxy is unavailable here; the process is not. A page that argues against certification sounds exactly like a page written by someone who could not get one.

copyDirectives.rule: Ban stock photography without exception
copyDirectives.do: Ship real photographs of tools, parts and the floor, including mid-process. If none exist yet, ship typography, diagrams and drawings instead.
copyDirectives.dont: Not one stock CNC spindle, not one anonymous robot arm, not one rendered factory.
copyDirectives.because: 'Uses stock photos' is named as the primary broker red flag in supplier vetting, and generic imagery is named by NN/g as an active trust destroyer. FEATURES.realProjectMedia is currently false — respect it.

copyDirectives.rule: Attach a note to every claim
copyDirectives.do: Keep the existing pattern in common.json where every trust item carries an explanatory note — the note is doing more work than the claim.
copyDirectives.dont: Do not ship a bare claim strip.
copyDirectives.because: The note is where judgement becomes visible. 'Tooling to 46 cavities' is a boast; 'high cavitation is a tooling discipline, not a machine specification' is an argument, and it converts a capability into a distinction.

copyDirectives.rule: State the response window as a deliverable, not a duration
copyDirectives.do: Say what arrives: feasibility direction, what is missing, and the next step. Say what does not: a final quotation.
copyDirectives.dont: Do not write 'fast response', '24/7', or 'we reply quickly'.
copyDirectives.because: Every site promises speed and no buyer believes any of them. A promise that names its own limits is the only kind that gets tested rather than discounted — and buyers do test it.

copyDirectives.rule: Put tooling ownership above warranty, and above almost everything else
copyDirectives.do: Give it its own block: property from payment, held in custody, marked with the customer's tool number, segregated, released on written request, CAD released on demand, no subcontracting without written approval, improvements belong to the tool's owner.
copyDirectives.dont: Do not bury it in an FAQ and do not leave it unsaid.
copyDirectives.because: 'Possession gives the factory leverage even when your ownership claim is strong.' It is the fear that keeps buyers with expensive incumbents, almost no competitor addresses it, and it is the one place a supplier without certification can outrank one with it. NOTE: this needs a new confirmed claim in claims.ts before it can ship.

copyDirectives.rule: Promise non-use, not confidentiality
copyDirectives.do: 'Your drawings, models and samples are not used to make the same part for anyone else, and are not shown to another customer.'
copyDirectives.dont: Do not write 'we respect your IP', '100% confidential', or claim enforceability anywhere.
copyDirectives.because: A conventional NDA covers disclosure and leaves competitive use open; non-use is the promise that addresses the actual fear, and it is legible without legal vocabulary.

copyDirectives.rule: Reduce first disclosure instead of promising legal protection
copyDirectives.do: 'You do not need to send a full CAD package to get a first answer. A photograph and one dimension is enough.'
copyDirectives.dont: Do not lead the IP section with the NDA.
copyDirectives.because: Cross-border enforcement is genuinely weak and a serious buyer's counsel knows it. Exposure reduction is verifiable by observation; legal remedy is not. Compete where the claim survives checking.

copyDirectives.rule: Never use an NDA to explain an absent portfolio
copyDirectives.do: Publish anonymised but specific engineering narratives — sector, part type, constraint, decision, reason.
copyDirectives.dont: Never write 'all our work is under NDA'.
copyDirectives.because: It is a recognised tell, flagged in claims.ts, and buyers discount it automatically because they have heard it from suppliers who had no history.

copyDirectives.rule: Give email equal weight to WhatsApp on every page, in every language
copyDirectives.do: Two controls, side by side, same visual weight. A named human address rather than info@.
copyDirectives.dont: Do not make WhatsApp the only route, do not make email the small grey link, and do not explain why an alternative exists.
copyDirectives.because: WhatsApp is blocked or degraded in Russia and China, marginal in Thailand, voice-blocked in the UAE, and unforwardable for European procurement. And some buyers simply will not put a foreign number in their phone — a concern that must be solved silently, because naming it makes it conspicuous.

copyDirectives.rule: Localise the channel, not only the words
copyDirectives.do: ru leads with email and phone. zh leads with WeChat. th leads with email. ar offers a telephone number for voice, never a WhatsApp call. tr and ur lead with WhatsApp. hy offers WhatsApp, Viber and Telegram.
copyDirectives.dont: Do not ship the same CTA component with the same channel priority across all nine locales.
copyDirectives.because: A CTA pointing at a blocked channel is not a weak CTA, it is no CTA — and it tells the buyer the supplier has never actually traded in their country.

copyDirectives.rule: Publish the cost structure, never the cost
copyDirectives.do: Explain what drives tooling price (cavitation, steel selection, sliders and lifters, finish class) and what drives part price (cycle time, wall thickness, runner type, material), plus the amortisation arithmetic.
copyDirectives.dont: No published prices, no 'starting from', no percentage savings — all prohibited.
copyDirectives.because: Pricing opacity is the single most damaging B2B trust gap, and NN/g's guidance is to give pricing indicators even without figures. An explained cost model is a pricing indicator, and it teaches the buyer to read every competitor's quote — a durable favour that costs nothing.

copyDirectives.rule: Say 'second-source readiness', never 'instant switchover'
copyDirectives.do: 'Most second-source work starts small on purpose — a duplicate tool, a qualification run, a share of the volume.'
copyDirectives.dont: Never claim reserved capacity, guaranteed availability, or immediate production of a part whose tool is in another country.
copyDirectives.because: Both are prohibited in claims.ts and both are implausible to anyone who has actually run a second-source qualification. Dual-source splits are typically 80/20 or 70/30 to the incumbent — treating the small share as the real job is what reads as competent.

copyDirectives.rule: Never criticise the incumbent
copyDirectives.do: 'Tell us what your current supplier does well. It is faster to match a known standard than to discover one.'
copyDirectives.dont: No comparison tables against unnamed competitors, no 'tired of late deliveries?', no implication that the buyer's current arrangement is naive.
copyDirectives.because: The buyer chose the incumbent and frequently still works with them. Attacking the incumbent attacks the buyer's judgement, and second-source buyers are seeking to add an option, not to admit an error.

copyDirectives.rule: Publish the schedule's shape, not its length
copyDirectives.do: Five stages, each with a gate, each gate naming what the buyer must supply or decide.
copyDirectives.dont: No lead-time figures anywhere — NEEDS-VERIFICATION.
copyDirectives.because: The drivers are more credible than the number, buyers discount published lead times anyway, and explaining what governs duration demonstrates exactly the judgement being shopped for.

copyDirectives.rule: Two fields to open; the full RFQ as an ungated gift
copyDirectives.do: First contact: what the part is, how to reach you, and a file attachment. Separately, publish a complete RFQ checklist, ungated, framed as 'every blank becomes an assumption, and assumptions get priced conservatively — here is the list, so you can price the same part fairly with anyone.'
copyDirectives.dont: No long form as the entry point, no required phone field, no gate, no registration.
copyDirectives.because: 4-field forms convert best and 4-to-3 lifts conversion ~50%, while multi-step converts 86% higher; and registration barriers before credibility destroy B2B trust. Splitting intake satisfies both the conversion data and the RFQ-completeness problem.

copyDirectives.rule: State a limit on every page
copyDirectives.do: Name one thing the company will not promise, cannot show yet, or does not do — in the same voice as everything else.
copyDirectives.dont: Do not present an unbounded capability set.
copyDirectives.because: Every supplier claims capability and almost none states a boundary. A stated boundary is unfakeable evidence that the other statements were filtered too. This is how the claim register's constraints become the site's voice rather than its handicap.

copyDirectives.rule: Every sentence must be traceable to a confirmed claim
copyDirectives.do: Before shipping any line of copy, map it to an id in claims.ts with status 'confirmed'. Run the FORBIDDEN_PHRASES lint on all nine locales, not only English.
copyDirectives.dont: Do not let a translator introduce a claim the English page does not make — this is the most likely route to an overclaim shipping unnoticed.
copyDirectives.because: Public research establishes facts about an industry and never about this company. Nine locales means nine chances for that boundary to be crossed by someone working without the register in front of them.

homepageImplications.coreStrategicPosition: This site cannot win on credentials, price, scale or references — all four are prohibited or unverified. It can only win on demonstrated engineering judgement and conspicuous operational honesty. Every design and copy decision should be tested against one question: does this make the reader more certain that a competent person is on the other end? That is the entire proposition, and it is a sufficient one — because it is precisely what certification is a proxy for, and because almost no competitor in this segment bothers to demonstrate it.

sectionBySection.job: Pass Gate 0 and serve the owner/CEO completely
sectionBySection.keep: The input list — an idea, a photograph, a physical sample, a drawing. It names what the buyer actually has rather than what a supplier would prefer, and it is the most differentiated sentence on the site.
sectionBySection.add: City and country, one line, unhedged. Working week if space allows.
sectionBySection.remove: Nothing. It is close to right.
sectionBySection.risk: If any stock imagery appears here the page dies before the copy is read.

sectionBySection.job: Convert the four confirmed facts into four arguments
sectionBySection.keep: The note-under-claim pattern. The notes are doing the persuasive work.
sectionBySection.add: Consider promoting tooling ownership into this strip once a confirmed claim exists — it is a larger buyer concern than warranty or delivery.
sectionBySection.remove: Resist any pressure to expand this into a stat wall. Four anchored facts outperform eight unanchored ones.
sectionBySection.risk: The response-window item is the site's most testable promise. If operations cannot keep 48 business hours, this strip becomes the site's biggest liability rather than its anchor.

sectionBySection.job: Serve the production manager on the surface and the engineer underneath
sectionBySection.keep: 'One chain, five stages, one accountable partner' and the framing that handovers are where projects fail — that is a genuine insight and it is the honest version of the single-accountability claim.
sectionBySection.add: Expandable engineering detail inside each stage, using the existing more/less toggle. This is where the certification gap gets closed, one specific decision at a time.
sectionBySection.remove: Any stage described in adjectives rather than decisions.
sectionBySection.risk: One technical error here loses the engineer permanently, and the engineer's verdict is delivered in one sentence to the person with the budget.

sectionBySection.section: Second source (recommended as a distinct block)
sectionBySection.job: Give procurement a small, reversible, approvable first step
sectionBySection.add: Readiness language, the duplicate-tool-instead-of-transfer argument, the qualification-run sequence, and an explicit statement that starting small is correct rather than provisional.
sectionBySection.avoid: Reserved-capacity claims, switchover promises, incumbent criticism.
sectionBySection.why: It matches how procurement actually onboards an unfamiliar overseas supplier — Conditional before Approved — and it asks for a decision the buyer can make without resolving every objection on the list first.

sectionBySection.job: Serve the procurement manager, who will scroll to find it
sectionBySection.add: How a quote is structured, how payment is staged against verifiable events, how tooling is owned and released, what the warranty framework is and why it is per project, and one ungated downloadable document.
sectionBySection.tone: Flat, unexcited, near-legal. This persona is repelled by enthusiasm and reassured by dryness.
sectionBySection.why: It is the only section that gives a procurement manager something to attach to a supplier file, which is often literally the deliverable of an audit-driven second-source search.

sectionBySection.job: Not lose a buyer who has already decided
sectionBySection.add: Two equally weighted channels, locale-aware in priority. A named human. A file-attachment route. Two fields maximum. The full RFQ checklist as an ungated download beside it, never as a gate.
sectionBySection.remove: Any required phone field. Any registration.
sectionBySection.risk: Every pending value in site.ts — WhatsApp number, email, phone, address, Telegram, WeChat — is a hole in this section. The email address and the physical address are the two blocking items; without them the site cannot pass Gate 0 or Gate 2 regardless of how good the copy is.
